text: With a paper chosen and a proposal written, this lesson is where you actually run it. Everything here is the lesson-seven reproduction playbook applied for real, wired into the repo structure and config system from chapter three and the tracking infrastructure from chapter four.

Four steps, in order. Run the official code first, completely unmodified, using their defaults and their checkpoint if one was released. Once that works, pull every setting it actually used — learning rate, optimizer betas, schedule, warmup, seed handling — into your own Hydra config, and let the code win over the paper's prose wherever the two disagree. Track every run in Weights and Biases or MLflow from the first attempt, not after something looks promising. And decide what counts as reproduced, using lesson seven's three tiers, before your run even finishes.

Nothing of your own runs until the official baseline script passes on your machine. Clone the authors' repository, install their exact dependencies, and run their own documented training command with their own default config. Your only goal here is confirming their code reproduces its own claimed number in your environment — if it doesn't, you've found an environment or dependency mismatch worth fixing before any of your own code gets involved at all.

Initialize your tracker with the full resolved config attached, not just the metrics, then log results every epoch so every run is self-describing on its own. A short comparison script at the end pulls your final number and the paper's reported number into the same place and prints the gap between them, so whether it reproduced has one clear, numeric answer instead of a feeling.
Once your number lands inside the tier you committed to, you've reproduced the result. Up next, lesson forty-four: designing one small, honest extension on top of it.
